name: Depilatory cream

image.caption: Depilatory Creams for back hair removal

lead: A depilatory cream is a topical product, usually containing thioglycolate salts, that dissolves hair at the skin surface so it can be wiped away. It is used on legs, underarms, chest and face to get smooth skin without a razor or pulling, and men's formulations exist for chest and body hair.

The chemistry weakens the keratin of the hair shaft so the hair scrapes off. Hair-removal reviews classify depilatories with shaving, removing the shaft only, so hair regrows within days. The largest body of clinical research is non-cosmetic: trials comparing cream with shaving for skin preparation before surgery.

paras: Users patch-test first, spread the cream over clean dry skin, wait the time on the label, then wipe or rinse it off. Results last a few days, similar to shaving, so it is repeated as needed.

Irritant contact dermatitis and chemical burns are the main risks, especially when left on longer than directed or used on broken or recently waxed skin. A pediatric case report documents a severe reaction after waxing and depilatory use. Patch testing is commonly advised.

angle.text: Users apply depilatory creams to the legs, underarms, chest or face to remove hair without razors or pulling. The chemical weakens hair keratin so hair wipes off at the surface, painlessly. Skin irritation is a recognized issue, which is why patch testing is commonly mentioned.

lead: A depilatory cream is a topical product that removes hair chemically. Most contain thioglycolate salts, which break the disulfide bonds of the keratin in the hair shaft so that the hair can be wiped or scraped from the skin surface.[1][2] It gives a smooth, hair-free look on the legs, underarms, bikini area, face and torso, including men's formulations for the chest and other body hair, and it does so without a blade, which suits people whose skin reacts to razors.

Hair removal reviews classify chemical depilatories, along with shaving, as depilation: removal of the hair shaft only, without removing the follicle.[3][4][5] Wikipedia notes that depilation does not destroy the dermal papilla, so hair grows back, and that results last several hours to several days.[2][5] Wikipedia's chemical depilatory article names Nair, Magic Shave and Veet among common brands and lists gel, cream, lotion, aerosol, roll-on and powder forms.[2]

The most extensive clinical research on depilatory creams is not cosmetic: a series of randomized and controlled trials compared cream depilation with shaving for preparing the skin before surgery, and Cochrane reviews have assessed these trials.[6][7][8][9][10][11][12] For cosmetic use, the literature consists mostly of case reports, laboratory studies of skin effects and general reviews.
infobox: Thioglycolate salts, about 5 to 6% calcium thioglycolate in a cream base[13][1][2]
pH about 12, kept by calcium or strontium hydroxide[2]

paras: Wikipedia describes the main reaction as thioglycolic acid reacting with cystine, the disulfide-linked amino acid in keratin, to give dithiodiglycolic acid and cysteine. Chemical depilatories contain about 5 to 6 percent calcium thioglycolate in a thick cream base to avoid runoff, with calcium or strontium hydroxide holding the pH near 12, and hair destruction takes about 10 minutes, after which the area is rinsed and conditioners can restore skin pH.[2] Older depilatories used sulfides such as strontium sulfide, replaced by thiols because of their odour.[2]

Depilatory creams are alkaline emulsions. The usual active ingredients are thioglycolate salts, such as calcium or potassium thioglycolate, which are commonly described as breaking the disulfide bonds that give keratin its strength, so that the softened hair can be wiped or scraped away. A 2008 laboratory study describes thioglycolate as the active ingredient of depilatory creams [1]. A French formulation paper described optimising a cold-process emulsion of calcium thioglycolate [13].

Because the chemistry acts on hair keratin and also affects skin keratin, the product is left on for a limited time specified by the manufacturer. A 2008 laboratory study applied a depilatory cream to fresh human skin for ten minutes and examined the changes in the stratum corneum; it characterised thioglycolate as a penetration enhancer and raised the possibility that it could increase permeation of other substances across skin [1]. A 2019 in vitro study similarly examined how physical and chemical hair removal methods affect skin barrier function [14].

Wikipedia reports that depilatory ointments or plasters were known to Greek and Roman writers as psilothrum, and that Jewish lore credits King Solomon with a depilatory of lime, water and orpiment (arsenic trisulfide).[2] The Hair removal article describes an abrasive paste of slaked lime, water, wood ash and orpiment as used in ancient times and still in rural India and Iran, and says chemical depilatories for women were introduced in 9th-century Al-Andalus by Ziryab, a claim it marks as lacking a citation.[5] Modern cream products replaced these with thioglycolate chemistry; Wikipedia lists Nair, Magic Shave and Veet among current brands.[2]

Hair removal reviews place depilatory creams in the same temporary category as shaving, with each method having advantages and disadvantages in efficacy and adverse events [4]. In the clinical trials of preoperative skin preparation, creams were studied as an alternative to shaving. A 1976 British Medical Journal trial of cream depilation versus routine shaving reported a similar wound infection rate in both groups, and found cream depilation effective, atraumatic and able to be self-administered, with a reduction in skin-surface bacteria and lower cost than shaving [15]. A randomized trial comparing razor shaving with a depilatory cream for preoperative preparation has also been published from Nigeria [10].
These trials measure infection outcomes in surgical patients, not the cosmetic quality or duration of hair removal.

Wikipedia's hair removal article places shaving and trimming as the most common depilation methods and notes that their results are short-lived compared with epilation, which lasts days to weeks; it does not directly compare creams with shaving.[5]

Irritant contact dermatitis is the main reported harm, and chemical burns are described in consumer and clinical guidance, particularly with application longer than directed or on broken or recently treated skin. A 2019 Pediatric Dermatology case report described severe irritant contact dermatitis after sequential waxing and depilatory cream use [16].

Laboratory work published in 2022 in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology examined the role of epidermal fatty acid-binding protein in acute skin inflammation induced by depilatories [17]. Product labels commonly advise a patch test before first use and avoidance of broken or irritated skin; these are label-based safety instructions rather than findings of the cited studies.

Wikipedia lists general hair-removal risks including inflammation, minor burns, lesions, scarring, ingrown hairs and folliculitis, without tying them specifically to creams.[5] A 2021 Cochrane review of 25 studies with 8,919 participants, cited in the same article, found that razors probably increase the risk of surgical site infection compared with clippers, hair removal cream or no removal.[5]

Cochrane reviews of preoperative hair removal (first published 2006, updated in 2011 and 2021) examined whether removing hair before surgery affects surgical site infection and whether the method matters [6][7][8][9]. Primary trials of depilatory creams date from 1966 onward [18][15][19][20][10], and a 2017 meta-analysis in the Journal of Clinical Nursing compared preoperative hair removal methods for surgical site infection [21]. Conclusions on cream versus other methods are given in the full reviews; the abstract available for the 2021 update describes its aim of assessing hair removal versus no removal, and the method, timing and setting of removal [6].
Chemical depilatories are also described by Wikipedia as indicated in the treatment of hirsutism in polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome.[2]

Depilatory creams are discussed in grooming circles as a painless, blade-free way to remove body hair from the chest, legs and other areas, often by people whose skin reacts to razors. Wikipedia reports that bodily depilation among men has grown in some Western subcultures, that footballers and road cyclists remove leg hair, and that competitive swimmers shave their bodies, and these athletic and physique contexts are where male hair removal is most often discussed.[5]

Bodybuilding and strength forums on T Nation discuss depilatories as one option among shaving and trimming for body hair. A 2003 poster suggested that someone could shave, trim or, if the skin is not very sensitive, use Nair or another depilatory cream; a 2001 poster described using Magic Shave, a cream depilatory, on face and head; and a 2008 poster told another member he might want to try a good depilatory cream.[22][23][24] In a 2009 thread a poster said Nair for Men was not bad but that an off-brand product he had not realised was extra strength made his skin bleed, illustrating why labels give a contact time.[25] A 2006 thread on shaving your own back includes a link to a back-hair shaving tool.[26]
Practitioners commonly describe patch-testing before first use, following the printed contact time and avoiding broken or freshly waxed skin, as the label advises.

Human trials of depilatory cream have mostly been done in surgical preparation. A 1966 Medical Journal of Australia trial, a 1976 British Medical Journal controlled trial, a 1983 American Journal of Surgery randomized trial comparing shaving with depilatory cream, a 2011 randomized trial in the Journal of Infection in Developing Countries and a 2020 randomized trial in the Nigerian Journal of Clinical Practice all examined cream depilation in patients [15][18][19][20][10]. Several Cochrane reviews pooled the evidence on preoperative hair removal [6][7][8][9]. For purely cosmetic use, a 2019 case report and laboratory skin-barrier studies are the available human-relevant literature [16][1][14].

lore.intro: Depilatory creams come up in grooming and bodybuilding forums as one option alongside shaving and trimming for body and facial hair, usually discussed in terms of skin tolerance and convenience.[22][23][24]
